subject_line: Rilke back in the auction rooms, twenty years on
email_body:
Dear Louise,

Returning to Rilke in The Second Cut two decades after The Cutting Room seems a rare thing to do with a narrator: he now has Grindr on his phone yet still drifts toward the darkened park, and the Glasgow around him has changed while his trade in other people's leftover possessions has not. I would love to ask what it was like to step back into his voice, and what the city had become in the meantime.

book_title: Catch the Moments as They Fly
subject_line: Rena, Bobby and thirty years of Kilmarnock
email_body:
Dear Zoë,

Catch the Moments as They Fly follows Rena and Bobby and their family through Kilmarnock from 1936 to 1966, so your home town carries a whole generation's story across the war and after. I'd like to ask how writing about a place you know so closely changed when you moved into historical fiction. I'm also curious whether the local history of your corner of Glasgow, which you are co-writing now, draws on the same instincts.

subject_line: From Caroline McNairn's paintings to SEKXPHRASTIKS
email_body:
Dear Jane,

Your first pamphlet, Border Thoughts, was a sequence of poems and elegies on the painter Caroline McNairn. Seven years later SEKXPHRASTIKS, from Dostoyevsky Wannabe, brought ekphrasis back into the title itself. I'd like to ask how writing toward paintings has changed for you between those two books, and how your work as a Woolf and modernism scholar sits alongside the poems on the page.

subject_line: Standing in front of Las Meninas with Velázquez
email_body:
Dear Amy,

Painter to the King begins and ends with Las Meninas and follows Velázquez through nearly four decades at Philip IV's court. It has almost no dialogue, and the Historical Novel Society reviewer described the narrator as someone standing in front of the paintings, trying to draw meaning out of them. I'd like to ask why you decided to stay so close to the documentary record while giving up dialogue altogether, and what looking at the paintings for so long taught you about sentences.

subject_line: Jack, Sonny and the 1957 whaling season
email_body:
Dear Malachy,

In That Beautiful Atlantic Waltz, Jack's solitary life in Shetland in the present runs against his father Sonny's 1957 season aboard a whaling ship. Like The Valley at the Centre of the World, the novel holds a whole community inside a small island setting. I'd like to ask how you came to the whaling material and why you paired a lonely older man with an unlikely friendship rather than telling a straight family history.

subject_line: Lockerbie, New York State and Small Acts of Love
email_body:
Dear Frances,

Small Acts of Love reopened the Citizens Theatre in 2025 after its long redevelopment. The play spans 36 years and follows a Scottish Borders town and a community in New York State who were thrown together by destruction and slowly built friendship through small kindnesses. I'd like to ask how you and Ricky Ross shared the storytelling between words and songs, and how you approached real grief that so many people still carry.

subject_line: From heat-death to a vanished god in Absence
email_body:
Dear Ali,

Absence, your first collection and the third book in Cheerio's poetry series, moves from the heat-death of the universe to a god who has disappeared to the end of a love affair. Abigail Parry called it "metaphysically gymnastic". I'd like to ask how you decided where the jokes belong in poems about loss, and what carried over from Hotel, the Verve pamphlet that won you an Eric Gregory Award.

subject_line: Iron Curtain after Gatsby and Karenina
email_body:
Dear Vesna,

Gorsky reimagined The Great Gatsby, and Monsieur Ka took up Sergei Karenin, Anna Karenina's son, and his life after the novel ends. After those two, Iron Curtain, published by Chatto & Windus in 2022, won the Momo Kapor prize and was shortlisted for the Society of Authors' Volcano prize. I'd like to ask whether writing it felt like a break from those borrowed frames, and how your poetry and memoir writing shape the way you build a novel.

subject_line: 360 five-line poems and A Marginal Sea
email_body:
Dear Zoë,

A Revolutionary Calendar sets out 360 five-line poems in twelve months of thirty, following the French Revolutionary calendar. After that, A Marginal Sea from Carcanet and Footnotes to Water, which won the Wales Book of the Year Poetry Award, return to water and edges. I'd like to ask how a strict calendar structure compares with the looser tidal shapes of the later book, and how your thinking on translation and relation, in your recent PN Review essay, feeds into the poems.

subject_line: Carrying Máirtín Ó Direáin into English
email_body:
Dear Frank,

Your translation of Máirtín Ó Direáin's Rogha Dánta / Selected Poems, published by Wake Forest in 2020, comes after many years with Cathal Ó Searcaigh's work, including Out in the Open and By the Hearth in Mín a' Leá, which you translated with Seamus Heaney and Denise Blake. I'd like to ask how Ó Direáin's voice asked different things of your English than Ó Searcaigh's did, and how translating sits alongside your own songs, poems and stories.

subject_line: Seventeen years from the Antarctic residency to Doc Wright
email_body:
Dear Jon,

You've said Lean Fall Stand repaid a 2004 Antarctic residency, when the ice forced your ship back to the Falklands, and that the novel took seventeen years to arrive. What began as a survival story became a book about Robert 'Doc' Wright's stroke and the aphasia group where he relearns language. I'd like to ask how talking with people living with aphasia, and their carers, changed the way you wrote sentences for him.

subject_line: Word-games and tonal swerves in Body Servant
email_body:
Dear Kit,

Body Servant came six years after Rain Down Can, your first Shearsman chapbook, and Rupert Loydell picked out its playful word-games and its unsettling shifts in tone. Between the two there was also the long-titled Knives Forks and Spoons pamphlet about the County Durham miner's granddaughter and the Harlan County miner's grandson. I'd like to ask how a childhood in Singapore, Turkey and England shows up in your ear for language, and how teaching poetry at DCU sits alongside writing it.

subject_line: Growing 'The Veil Thins' from story into novel
email_body:
Dear Fiona,

'The Veil Thins' has followed an unusual path. An earlier version, 'The veil is thinning out', was runner-up in the Seán Ó Faoláin competition, and the story then won the Goldenberg Prize for Fiction in 2025. Now the novel you are building from it is among the twelve winners of the Irish Writers' Centre debut novel competition. I'd like to ask what the story kept insisting on that made it want to become a novel, and how teaching at SETU feeds your writing.

subject_line: Ben's voice from the rehab clinic in White City
email_body:
Dear Kevin,

White City is told by Ben, the 27-year-old son of a retired South Dublin banker, speaking from a rehab clinic, and reviewers noted how easily the book moves between comedy and sincerity. It was shortlisted for the 2022 Kerry Group Novel of the Year. I'd like to ask how you kept a narrator with that much privilege and self-pity funny without letting him off the hook, and how teaching at the Oscar Wilde Centre affects the way you revise.

subject_line: James, Luke and the northern village in Open, Heaven
email_body:
Dear Seán,

Open, Heaven, your first novel, follows James, a shy sixteen-year-old in a remote village in the north of England, whose fixation on the older Luke turns into an obsession he cannot act on. BookBrowse's reviewer singled out your command of language, which makes sense for a poet's first long prose fiction. I'd like to ask how your habits as a poet carried over into the novel, and what prose allowed you to do with the silence between the two boys.
